headline: High prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared VS Code filesystem and broad network/tool access; Cline can feed untrusted workspace content into transformers pipelines.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cline runs in a VS Code workspace with shared state via filesystem and can use MCP, while transformers reads files and processes Python/model/example inputs. That creates a direct path for attacker-controlled workspace content from agent_a to influence agent_b as instructions or code. The pair lacks provenance tracking or isolation in the profiles.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes workspace files produced by agent_a without provenance checks
IF agent_a writes prompt-like content into shared workspace files
IF MCP content is bridged into the same workspace
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP for untrusted content paths
Add provenance tags to files before B reads them
Require manual review of any agent_a-generated instructions
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem isolation or sandbox mounts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write the same workspace files, and both have broad network egress. Cline touches source code and browser screenshots; transformers touches text, audio, images, video, and multimodal data. Shared workspace plus file-reading means sensitive content can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs, though the profiles do not show automatic third-party exfiltration beyond configured APIs.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace
IF either agent serializes file contents into prompts or outputs
IF browser screenshots or multimodal inputs contain secrets
mitigations: Use separate least-privilege workspaces
Redact secrets before either agent reads files
Restrict network egress to approved endpoints
Review outputs before sharing externally
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on workspace reads

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. Cline also modifies git state, while transformers can operate on Python/model files; concurrent writes to the same workspace or repo can corrupt state or overwrite each other. The shared filesystem concurrency model makes this conflict plausible by default.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repo
IF either agent edits files without external locking
IF concurrent package installs or subprocesses touch shared state
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Pause one agent during the other's write phase
Use git locks or serialized commits
Limit one agent to read-only mode during analysis
requires-engineering: add workspace-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cline can generate code, browser-derived content, and tool outputs that transformers may ingest through files or pipelines. The profiles do not show a verification gate between them, so B may treat A’s output as authoritative. However, B is a document-processing framework rather than an autonomous action agent, so the blast radius is lower than high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-generated files as ground truth
IF agent_a writes unverified facts into shared artifacts
IF downstream scripts act on B's processed outputs
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B consumes A outputs
Mark A-generated files as untrusted
Require citations or source links for factual claims
Keep A and B outputs in separate folders
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so a compliance breach is not established. The only concrete compliance-relevant fact is that Cline handles model provider API keys and browser screenshots, while transformers is a general open-source framework with no stated compliance controls. Uncertainty stays low because the mismatch is not evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through either agent without a separate policy
IF screenshots or secrets are stored in a jurisdictionally restricted workspace
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in the shared workspace
Document retention and deletion rules
Store secrets outside agent-accessible files
Review vendor compliance claims before deployment
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
